lede: Everything in Topic 14, split into two bands. sections.title: The three states in the kinetic model: arrangement and movement

parts.title: Arrangement and movement
parts.html:
SolidLiquidGas
Arrangementregular pattern (lattice), touching, fixed positionsirregular, touching, no fixed positionsrandom, far apart (about ten times the particle size), no pattern
Movementvibrate about fixed positionsmove around / slide past each other in random directions, with a range of speeds, colliding with each othermove fast, in straight lines, in random directions, colliding with each other and the walls

The June 2023 report (Q3(c)(ii), the motion of particles in a liquid): "the particles flow over each other" scored; "move freely" is the "random" mark — one of four credited points (random; a range of speeds; collide with each other; faster than in a solid) — so a second, different point about the motion is needed for the second mark ("random speeds" on its own scores 1); imprecise phrases such as "with lots of energy", bulk properties ("they take the shape of the container") and descriptions of melting scored nothing — the question was about the motion, not the change. The June 2025 report (Q5(b), liquid wax freezing): "now only vibrate in fixed positions" was full marks; "no longer move past each other" and "slow down / lose energy" scored; "become closer together" is arrangement, not motion, and "is not enough for a mark".

parts.title: Liquid to solid
parts.question: Liquid wax cools and becomes solid. Describe the change in the motion of the wax particles. (2 marks)
steps: In the liquid the particles move around, flowing over each other; as the wax cools they slow down (lose kinetic energy).
In the solid they no longer move past each other: they only vibrate about fixed positions.

questions.text: Describe the arrangement and movement of the particles in a gas. (2)
questions.model:
• Arrangement: far apart, in random positions with no pattern.
  • Movement: moving fast in straight lines in random directions (colliding with each other and the container).

questions.text: Which statement about particles in a liquid would score for 'describe the motion'?
options: They take the shape of the container
They move around and flow over each other
questions.explain: 2023: 'flow over each other' scored — the scheme also credits 'random', 'a range of speeds' and 'collide with each other'; the other options are bulk properties, vague energy or arrangement.

questions.text: Explain, using the particle model, why a solid has a fixed shape but a liquid does not. (2)
questions.model:
• In a solid the particles are held in fixed positions (only vibrating), so the solid keeps its shape.
  • In a liquid the particles are still touching but can move around / flow over each other, so the liquid takes the shape of its container.

questions.text: Why can a gas be compressed easily but a liquid cannot?
options: Gas particles are far apart with empty space between them; liquid particles are already touching
questions.explain: Compression closes up the gaps; a liquid has none to close.

questions.text: Ice is heated until it melts. Describe the change in the motion of the particles. (2)
questions.model:
• In the ice the particles vibrate about fixed positions; as it is heated they vibrate more (gain energy).
  • At melting they leave their fixed positions and can move around / flow over each other (still touching).

checklist: Describe the arrangement of particles in a solid, a liquid and a gas
Describe the movement of particles in each state in the words that score
When asked for differences, write each point for both states ('in a solid … but in a liquid …') — a one-sided statement does not score after the first mark (Nov 2021 2H Q3(a))
Explain a bulk property (fixed shape, flows, fills its container) from the particle picture
sections.blurb: Every state-of-matter answer has two halves — how the particles are arranged and how they move — and the marks are usually on the movement. Solids vibrate about fixed positions; liquid particles are still touching but move around and flow over each other; gas particles are far apart and move fast in straight lines in all directions.

sections.title: Density: mass per unit volume, in SI units

parts.title: The equation and its units
parts.html:
Density is the mass per unit volume: $\rho = m \div V$, in kg/m³ when the mass is in kg and the volume in m³. The same substance has the same density whatever the size of the sample — half a brick has half the mass and half the volume, so the same density. Water is about 1000 kg/m³ (1 g/cm³), air about 1.2 kg/m³, steel about 7900 kg/m³.

Units: the June 2023 report (Q3(b)) — candidates converted the given kg and m³ into g and cm³ "and often used incorrect powers of ten"; "candidates are advised to use SI units in all calculations unless instructed specifically to convert". When you must convert: 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³ (because $1 \text{ m}^3 = 1\,000\,000 \text{ cm}^3$ and $1 \text{ kg} = 1000 \text{ g}$), so multiply g/cm³ by 1000 to get kg/m³. 1 cm³ = 1 × 10⁻⁶ m³; 1 litre = 1000 cm³ = 0.001 m³.

Rounding: the June 2025 report (Q5(c)(i)) — many rounded a volume of 0.0047 m³ to 0.005 m³, which was "unnecessary and actually poor practice"; give the answer to the same number of significant figures as the data (two, there). A volume is also a check on sense: a small block of metal is a few cm³, i.e. a few ×10⁻⁶ m³.

parts.title: Volume from density
parts.question: A piece of wax has a mass of 4.2 kg and a density of 900 kg/m³. Calculate its volume. (2 marks)
steps: $\rho = m \div V$, so $V = m \div \rho = 4.2 \div 900$.
$V = 0.0047$ m³ (2 s.f., matching the data — not 0.005).

questions.text: A copper block has a mass of 445 g and a volume of 50 cm³. Calculate its density in g/cm³.
questions.hint: $\rho = m \div V$ in the units given.

questions.text: Convert 8.9 g/cm³ into kg/m³.
A cylinder of volume 0.0080 m³ has a density of 7900 kg/m³. Calculate its mass.
walkthrough: Units: kg (63.2 to 2 s.f., matching the data)

questions.text: A bottle holds 0.75 litres of oil of density 920 kg/m³. Calculate the mass of the oil.
A question gives a mass in kg and a volume in m³. The best plan is…
options: convert both to g and cm³ first
use them as they are: SI units in, kg/m³ out
questions.explain: 2023 report: use SI units unless told to convert.

checklist: Use $\rho = m/V$ to find density, mass or volume
Work in SI units (kg, m³) and convert g/cm³ ↔ kg/m³ when asked
Round to the significant figures of the data, not to one figure
sections.blurb: Density is mass divided by volume: how much mass is packed into each cubic metre. The equation is on the list; the marks are for the units — work in kilograms and cubic metres unless the question says otherwise — and for sensible rounding.

sections.title: The density core practical: regular solid, irregular solid, liquid
equations: \text{volume: ruler, or displacement, or the cylinder scale}

parts.title: The three methods
parts.html:
ObjectMassVolumeAccuracy
Regular solid (block, cylinder)balancemeasure length, width and height with a ruler (or vernier callipers); $V = l \times w \times h$measure each side in several places and average; zero the balance first
Irregular solid (stone, key)balancepour water into a measuring cylinder and read the volume; lower the object in so it is completely under the water; read the new volume; volume = after − beforeread the bottom of the meniscus at eye level; lower gently (no splashing); dry the object before weighing it, or weigh it first
Liquidput an empty measuring cylinder on the balance and zero it (or record its mass); pour in the liquid; the reading is the liquid's mass (or subtract)read the volume from the cylinder's scaleuse a large volume (a small percentage error); read the meniscus at eye level

Then $\rho = m \div V$ for each. The June 2023 report (Q3(d), volume of an irregular piece of metal, 2 marks): any two of measure the water volume before adding the metal, make sure all the metal is immersed, subtract the initial from the final volume — "many candidates scored full marks". But "describing a displacement (Eureka) can … scored nothing" — the question had given a measuring cylinder, and the can is a different method (collect the overflow and measure that; useful for an object too big for a cylinder, but not the one asked for); and measurements not relevant to volume, such as the metal's mass, were ignored — as were "repeat and average", spillage and the meniscus: in that 2-mark volume question only the before-reading, full immersion and the subtraction scored. The June 2024 scheme (Q3(d)) had students read a volume off a scale before and after (1350 and 1750 cm³, each accepted within a range) and subtract: 400 cm³.

parts.title: The irregular solid
parts.question: Describe how to find the volume of a small irregular piece of metal using a measuring cylinder. (3 marks)
steps: Pour water into the measuring cylinder and read the volume (bottom of the meniscus, at eye level).
Lower the metal gently into the water so that it is completely submerged, and read the new volume.
The volume of the metal is the difference: final reading − initial reading.

questions.text: Describe how to find the density of a small stone. (4)
questions.model:
• Measure the stone's mass on a balance.
  • Pour water into a measuring cylinder and read the volume.
  • Lower the stone in so it is fully under the water; read the new volume; volume = new − old.
  • Density = mass ÷ volume ($\rho = m / V$). Accuracy (the fourth mark in June 2019 2H Q7(a)): read the level at eye level, and use a measuring cylinder only a little wider than the stone (or several stones together) so the rise is large — "repeat and average" is ignored.

questions.text: Which measurement is NOT needed to find the volume of an irregular solid by the measuring-cylinder method?
options: The water volume before the object goes in
The water volume after the object goes in
That the object is fully under the water
questions.explain: 2023 scheme: 'ignore other measurements such as mass' — the mass is not wrong, it is not a volume measurement, so it scores nothing in a volume question.

questions.text: Describe how to find the density of a liquid. (3)
questions.model:
• Put an empty measuring cylinder on a balance and zero it (or record its mass).
  • Pour in the liquid: the balance gives the liquid's mass (subtracting the empty cylinder if needed); read the volume from the cylinder scale.
  • Density = mass ÷ volume.

questions.text: A measuring cylinder reads 45 cm³. A stone of mass 52 g is lowered in and the reading becomes 65 cm³. Calculate the density of the stone.
Which is an accuracy improvement for the regular-block method?
options: Measure each dimension at several places along it (and use the mean), or use a larger block
questions.explain: A bare 'repeat the readings' is ignored in the density method schemes (2019, 2023); measuring at several places along a side checks it is uniform, and a larger block makes the percentage error smaller.

checklist: Describe how to find the density of a regular solid, an irregular solid and a liquid
Describe the measuring-cylinder method for an irregular solid in the words that score
State one accuracy point for each method
sections.blurb: Three objects, three ways to find the volume, one balance for the mass. A regular block: measure its sides and multiply. An irregular solid: the rise in water level in a measuring cylinder. A liquid: pour a measured volume into a cylinder on a balance. When the question gives you a measuring cylinder, describe that method: in 2023 a displacement can scored nothing.

sections.title: Why solids are denser than liquids than gases: particle spacing

parts.title: The spacing argument
parts.html:
Density is mass per unit volume, and the particles of one substance all have the same mass, so density depends only on how closely the particles are packed — how many there are in each cubic metre. In a gas the particles are far apart (most of the volume is empty space), so there are far fewer in each m³: a gas is roughly a thousand times less dense than the liquid (steam about 0.6 kg/m³, water 1000 kg/m³). In a liquid and a solid the particles are touching, so the densities are similar; in most substances the solid's regular packing is slightly closer than the liquid's irregular packing, so the solid is a little denser and sinks in its own liquid. The June 2024 scheme (Q3(b), 2 marks): "density of solid is greater than liquid"; "(because) the distance between particles in the solid is less" — "particles are closer", "more tightly packed" and "more particles per unit volume" all accepted. The June 2025 question (Q5(c)(ii)) did it with data: the same mass of wax had a smaller volume as a solid than as a liquid.

The famous exception: ice is less dense than water (920 against 1000 kg/m³), because water molecules in ice are held in an open lattice with more space between them than in the liquid — which is why ice floats and pipes burst. The spec wants the general rule; the exception is worth knowing because questions use it.

parts.title: Solid and liquid wax
parts.question: Explain why solid wax is denser than liquid wax. (2 marks)
steps: In the solid the particles are packed in a regular pattern with the particle spacing smaller than in the liquid — more particles in each unit of volume.
Density is mass per unit volume and the particles have the same mass, so the solid, with more particles per m³, is denser (the same mass of wax takes up a smaller volume as a solid).

questions.text: Explain, in terms of particles, why steam is much less dense than water. (2)
questions.model:
• In steam (a gas) the particles are far apart, with mostly empty space between them; in water they are touching.
  • So there are far fewer particles per unit volume in steam, and density is mass per unit volume.

questions.text: A solid is usually denser than its liquid because…
options: its particles are closer together (more particles per unit volume)
questions.explain: Same particles, closer packing.

questions.text: Roughly how do the densities of a substance as a gas and as a liquid compare?
options: The gas is about a thousand times less dense
The gas is twice as dense
The gas is ten times less dense
questions.explain: Particles about ten times further apart in each direction: a thousand times fewer per m³.

questions.text: A table shows 0.050 kg of a substance has a volume of 60 cm³ as a solid and 65 cm³ as a liquid. Use the data to compare the two densities. (1)
questions.model: • The same mass occupies a smaller volume as a solid (60 cm³ against 65 cm³), so the solid is denser (0.83 against 0.77 g/cm³).

questions.text: Ice floats on water because…
options: ice is less dense than water — its molecules are held further apart in the solid lattice
questions.explain: The exception to the rule, and why pipes burst.

checklist: Explain why a gas is much less dense than the same substance as a liquid or solid
Explain why a solid is usually slightly denser than its liquid
State the exception: ice is less dense than water
sections.blurb: The same particles, packed differently. In a solid and a liquid they are touching, so the densities are similar (the solid usually a little higher); in a gas they are far apart, so a gas is about a thousand times less dense. The mark is for the spacing — the number of particles per unit volume — not for the particles being heavier.

sections.title: Changes of state: the six names, mass conserved, physical not chemical

parts.title: The six changes, and why they are physical
parts.html:
ChangeFrom → toEnergy
Meltingsolid → liquidtaken in (at the melting point)
Freezing (solidifying)liquid → solidgiven out (at the same temperature, the freezing point)
Boilingliquid → gas, throughout the liquid, at the boiling pointtaken in
Evaporatingliquid → gas, from the surface only, at any temperaturetaken in (which is why evaporation cools)
Condensinggas → liquidgiven out
Sublimatingsolid → gas directly (dry ice, iodine); gas → solid is depositiontaken in

Mass is conserved: the particles are not created, destroyed or changed — the same number of the same particles, just arranged and moving differently — so the mass after a change of state equals the mass before (a sealed flask of ice weighs the same once it has melted). These are physical changes: reverse the change (freeze the water again) and the substance recovers its original properties. Many chemical changes make new substances (burning wood, rusting iron) and cannot be reversed by reversing the conditions. The June 2024 paper (Q9(a)) asked which change is solid → gas: sublimation (not melting, freezing or condensation).

parts.title: Physical or chemical?
parts.question: Explain why melting ice is a physical change but burning wood is a chemical change. (3 marks)
steps: Melting ice: the water particles are unchanged — only their arrangement and movement change — so the mass is conserved…
…and the change is reversible: freeze the water and you get ice with its original properties back.
Burning wood makes new substances (ash, carbon dioxide, water vapour) with different properties; the wood cannot be recovered by reversing the conditions, so it is a chemical change.

questions.text: The change from a solid directly to a gas is called…
questions.explain: 2024 Q9(a). Dry ice (solid CO₂) does it at room temperature.

questions.text: A sealed container holds 50 g of ice. The ice melts. State the mass of the water and explain your answer. (2)
questions.model:
• 50 g: mass is conserved.
  • The same particles are present before and after — none are created or destroyed, they are only arranged and moving differently.

questions.text: Which is the difference between boiling and evaporating?
options: Boiling needs energy, evaporating does not
Boiling happens throughout the liquid at the boiling point; evaporating happens only at the surface, at any temperature
questions.explain: Both liquid → gas; boiling is at one temperature, through the bulk.

questions.text: State what is meant by a physical change, and give one way it differs from a chemical change. (2)
questions.model:
• A change in which the substance is not changed into a new substance (only its state, arrangement or movement of particles) — e.g. melting, boiling.
  • It is reversible: the material recovers its original properties when the change is reversed; a chemical change makes new substances.

questions.text: Which change gives energy OUT to the surroundings?
questions.explain: Condensing and freezing release the energy that boiling and melting took in.

checklist: Name the six changes of state and which way each goes
State that mass is conserved in a change of state, and why
Explain the difference between a physical change and a chemical change
sections.blurb: Melting, freezing, boiling (and evaporating), condensing and sublimating are physical changes: the particles are the same particles, so mass is conserved, and the substance gets its original properties back if the change is reversed — unlike many chemical changes, which make new substances.

sections.title: Heating a system: temperature rise or change of state; specific heat capacity and specific latent heat
equations: \text{SLH: energy per kg to change state, no temperature change}

parts.title: Two things heating can do
parts.html:
Heating transfers energy into the thermal store of a system — its internal energy, the total kinetic and potential energy of its particles. That energy does one of two things:

Raising the temperatureChanging the state
What the particles domove faster (vibrate more in a solid): their kinetic energy increasesbreak away from their neighbours / separate: their potential energy increases, the kinetic energy does not
Temperaturerisesstays constant at the melting or boiling point while the change happens
Quantityspecific heat capacity, $c$specific latent heat, $L$
Definition (learn the sentence)the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of the substance by 1 °C (unit J/kg °C)the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of the substance without a change in temperature (unit J/kg)
Water4200 J/kg °C (large — water is slow to heat and slow to cool)fusion (melting) 334 000 J/kg; vaporisation (boiling) 2 260 000 J/kg

The difference (14.7): specific heat capacity is about a temperature change with no change of state; specific latent heat is about a change of state with no temperature change. "Latent" means hidden — the energy goes in but the thermometer does not move. Each change has its own latent heat: fusion for melting/freezing, vaporisation for boiling/condensing, and the energy comes back out when the change reverses.

parts.title: The two definitions
parts.question: Define specific heat capacity and specific latent heat, and state the difference between them. (3 marks)
steps: Specific heat capacity: the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C.
Specific latent heat: the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of a substance with no change in temperature.
The difference: one is for a temperature change (the particles speed up), the other for a change of state at constant temperature (the particles separate, potential energy rises).

questions.text: State what is meant by the specific heat capacity of a substance. (1)
questions.model: • The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of the substance by 1 °C.

questions.text: State what is meant by the specific latent heat of vaporisation of water. (1)
questions.model: • The energy needed to change 1 kg of water from liquid to gas (boil it) without a change in temperature.

questions.text: While a substance is melting, the energy supplied…
options: increases the kinetic energy of the particles
increases the potential energy of the particles as they break from their fixed positions, with no temperature change
questions.explain: Latent: the thermometer does not move.

questions.text: Explain the difference between specific heat capacity and specific latent heat. (2)
questions.model:
• Specific heat capacity is the energy per kg to change the temperature by 1 °C, with no change of state.
  • Specific latent heat is the energy per kg to change the state, with no change in temperature.

questions.text: Water has a large specific heat capacity (4200 J/kg °C). This means that…
options: a lot of energy is needed to raise its temperature, so it heats up and cools down slowly
water has a high melting point
questions.explain: Why the sea moderates the climate and why central heating uses water.

checklist: Explain what heating does to the energy stored in a system, and the two things it can do
Define specific heat capacity and specific latent heat in the mark-scheme words
Explain the difference between them: temperature change vs change of state
sections.blurb: Heating a system increases the energy stored in it. That energy either raises the temperature (the particles move faster — more kinetic energy) or changes the state at a constant temperature (the particles' bonds are loosened or broken — more potential energy). Specific heat capacity measures the first per kilogram per degree; specific latent heat measures the second per kilogram.

sections.title: The two thermal equations, and when each applies

parts.title: Choosing the equation
parts.html:
The question says…EquationWatch
temperature rises / falls from … to …$\Delta Q = m c \Delta\theta$$\Delta\theta$ is the change (final − initial); the same number in °C or K — and if the question asks for a temperature, finish: 100 − 80 = 20 °C (an answer of 80 scored 2 of 3 in June 2019 2H Q7(b)(i))
melts / freezes / boils / condenses, at a constant temperature$Q = m L$no $\Delta\theta$ at all; use the latent heat for the right change (fusion or vaporisation)

The June 2024 scheme: Q3(c), $Q = m L$ for a change of state — substitution (1), evaluation (1), $1.36 \times 10^5$ J; Q9(c)(i), $\Delta\theta = \Delta Q \div (m c)$ — rearrangement and substitution (1), evaluation (1), 42 °C. Grams must become kilograms before substituting (250 g = 0.25 kg), and a latent heat of 334 000 J/kg is often written 334 kJ/kg — convert, or keep the kJ and remember the answer is in kJ.

parts.title: Ice to warm water
parts.question: 0.20 kg of ice at 0 °C is turned into water at 30 °C. Specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 334 000 J/kg; specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg °C. Calculate the total energy needed. (4 marks)
steps: Melt the ice (no temperature change): $Q = m L = 0.20 \times 334\,000 = 66\,800$ J.
Warm the water from 0 °C to 30 °C: $\Delta\theta = 30$ °C.
$\Delta Q = m c \Delta\theta = 0.20 \times 4200 \times 30 = 25\,200$ J.

questions.text: Calculate the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1.5 kg of water from 20 °C to 60 °C. ($c = 4200$ J/kg °C)
Calculate the energy needed to boil 0.50 kg of water that is already at 100 °C. ($L = 2\,260\,000$ J/kg)
questions.hint: A change of state at constant temperature: $Q = m L$.

questions.text: A 2.0 kg aluminium block ($c = 900$ J/kg °C) receives 36 000 J. Calculate its temperature rise.
250 g of ice at 0 °C melts and the water warms to 10 °C. Calculate the total energy needed. ($L = 334\,000$ J/kg, $c = 4200$ J/kg °C)
questions.hint: 250 g = 0.25 kg; melt, then warm; add.

questions.text: Steam at 100 °C condenses to water at 100 °C. Which equation gives the energy released?
options: $Q = m L$ with the latent heat of vaporisation
$Q = m L$ with the latent heat of fusion
questions.explain: Change of state at constant temperature; vaporisation for gas ↔ liquid.

checklist: Use $\Delta Q = m c \Delta \theta$ for a temperature change and $Q = m L$ for a change of state
Split a mixed problem into stages and add the energies
Use the temperature change, not the temperature, and the mass in kg
sections.blurb: Temperature change: $\Delta Q = m c \Delta \theta$. Change of state: $Q = m L$. A problem that does both — ice at −10 °C to water at 20 °C — is three steps added together. Both equations are on the list; the marks are for choosing the right one for each stage, using Δθ (a change, the same in °C or K) and keeping the mass in kilograms.

sections.title: Reducing unwanted energy transfer: thermal insulation

parts.title: How insulation works
parts.html:
Energy is transferred from a hot object to its cooler surroundings by heating — conduction through solids, convection in fluids, radiation. Thermal insulation slows this down: an insulator has a low thermal conductivity, and most good insulators work by trapping air in small pockets (foam, fibreglass, wool, feathers, bubble wrap), because still air is a poor conductor and the pockets stop it convecting. Thicker insulation, more layers and a smaller surface area all reduce the rate of transfer. The vacuum flask removes the air altogether between its double walls (no conduction or convection) and silvers the surfaces (less radiation).

The spec's examples: lagging a hot-water tank or pipes, loft insulation, cavity-wall insulation, double glazing (a trapped layer of air or gas between the panes), a lid on a beaker, a cup sleeve. In the SHC practical (T6) the beaker is lagged so that nearly all the heater's energy goes into the water. The June 2025 report (Q3(d)): students explained a thick cable's plastic coating as "thermal insulation to prevent energy loss" — wrong: "wasted heat can only be reduced by lowering resistance, and insulation at best only reduces transfer of that heat to the air". The plastic is electrical insulation (Topic 10); thermal insulation is about reducing transfer by heating.

parts.title: The hot drink
parts.question: A cafe serves hot drinks in cups with a cardboard sleeve and a lid. Explain how these reduce the rate at which the drink cools. (3 marks)
steps: The sleeve is a thermal insulator with a low thermal conductivity (corrugated card traps air), so less energy is conducted through the side of the cup each second.
The lid stops the hot vapour and air above the drink escaping — it reduces transfer by convection and by evaporation from the surface.
With less energy transferred to the surroundings each second, the drink's temperature falls more slowly.

questions.text: Explain how loft insulation reduces the rate of energy transfer out of a house. (2)
questions.model:
• The fibreglass or wool has a low thermal conductivity and traps air in small pockets (air is a poor conductor and cannot convect in the pockets).
  • So energy is conducted through the roof space more slowly: less energy transferred to the outside each second.

questions.text: A thick plastic coating on an electrical cable is…
options: thermal insulation that stops the cable wasting energy
electrical insulation; wasted energy in the cable is reduced by lowering its resistance, not by the coating
questions.explain: 2025 report: the coating does not reduce the heating; a lower resistance does.

questions.text: A vacuum flask keeps a drink hot. Explain how the vacuum between its double walls helps. (2)
questions.model:
• There are no particles in a vacuum, so energy cannot be transferred across the gap by conduction or convection.
  • Only radiation can cross it, and the silvered surfaces reduce that — so the drink loses energy very slowly.

questions.text: Which change would increase the rate at which a beaker of hot water cools?
options: Pouring the water into a wide shallow dish
Standing it on a cork mat
questions.explain: A larger surface area in contact with the air: faster transfer.

questions.text: Why does double glazing use two panes with a gap rather than one thick pane?
options: Glass is a good conductor, so thicker glass helps little; the trapped air (or gas) between the panes has a low thermal conductivity
questions.explain: The gap is the insulator.

checklist: Explain how insulation reduces unwanted energy transfer
Give examples: lagging, loft insulation, double glazing, a vacuum flask
Distinguish thermal insulation from electrical insulation
sections.blurb: Unwanted transfer by heating is reduced with insulation: a material of low thermal conductivity, usually one that traps air (foam, fibreglass, feathers, double glazing) so that conduction and convection are both cut down. The 2025 examiners saw students apply the word to a cable's plastic coating — that insulation is electrical, not thermal.

sections.title: Gas pressure from particle collisions, and what heating does to it

parts.title: The collision chain
parts.html:
Why a gas has a pressure (14.12): the particles move fast and randomly; they collide with the walls of the container; each collision exerts a force on the wall (the particle's momentum is changed, so the wall pushes it and it pushes the wall — Topic 2); with billions of collisions each second the total force on each unit of area is steady — that is the pressure.

Heating a fixed mass of gas at constant volume (14.13): the particles gain kinetic energy and move faster (the average speed rises); so they collide with the walls more often (more collisions per second) and harder (each collision exerts a larger force); so the total force on the walls increases; so the pressure increases. Cool it and everything reverses. The chain needs both "more frequent" and "harder" (greater force per collision) for full marks, and it must say the walls — "the particles bump into each other more" earns nothing, because collisions between particles do not push on the container.

parts.title: A sealed can in the sun
parts.question: A sealed can of gas is left in the sun and warms up. Explain why the pressure inside the can increases. (3 marks)
steps: The gas particles move faster — a greater average speed means a greater average kinetic energy ($KE = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$, a link in the June 2022 2H Q9(c) indicative content).
So they collide with the walls of the can more frequently and with more force each time (harder).
The volume is fixed, so the total force on the walls increases and the area is unchanged: the pressure increases ($p = F \div A$).

questions.text: Explain how the particles of a gas produce a pressure on the walls of their container. (3)
questions.model:
• The particles move fast and randomly and collide with the walls.
  • Each collision exerts a force on the wall.
  • The total force of all the collisions per unit area of wall is the pressure.

questions.text: A fixed mass of gas at constant volume is cooled. Its pressure…
options: decreases, because the particles move more slowly and hit the walls less often and less hard
questions.explain: The chain in reverse.

questions.text: Which statement is not a link in the gas-pressure chain?
options: The particles collide with the walls
The particles collide with each other more often
Each collision exerts a force on the wall
The particles move faster when heated
questions.explain: The collisions that matter for pressure are the ones with the walls; 'collide with each other' is not one of the credited points in a pressure explanation (it does score in a 'describe the motion' question, 2023).

questions.text: A sealed rigid container of gas is heated from 20 °C to 80 °C. Explain the effect on the pressure. (3)
questions.model:
• The particles move faster (greater average speed / kinetic energy).
  • So they hit the walls more often and harder (greater force per collision).
  • The volume is constant, so the total force per unit area — the pressure — increases.

questions.text: A sealed can is taken from a cold room into a warm room; its volume does not change (2024 Q9(b)). Which quantity does NOT increase?
options: The mean speed of the particles
The mean distance between the particles
The mean size of the momentum of the particles
questions.explain: Constant volume and the same number of particles: the spacing cannot change.

checklist: Explain the pressure of a gas in terms of particle collisions
Explain why heating a fixed mass of gas at constant volume increases its pressure
Write the chain in the mark-scheme words: faster → more frequent and harder collisions → greater force → greater pressure
sections.blurb: Gas particles move fast and randomly and collide with the walls of their container; each collision exerts a small force on the wall, and the total force per unit area is the pressure. Heat the gas (at constant volume) and the particles move faster, so they hit the walls more often and harder, and the pressure rises.

sections.title: Absolute zero and the kelvin scale

parts.title: The scale that starts at the bottom
parts.html:
As a gas is cooled its particles move more and more slowly and its pressure falls. Extrapolating, at −273 °C the particles would have the least possible movement (the lowest possible energy) and the pressure would be zero: this is absolute zero, the lowest temperature there can be — nothing can be colder, because there is no movement left to take away. The spec's words (14.14): absolute zero, −273 °C, "in terms of the lack of movement of particles".

The kelvin scale starts there: 0 K = −273 °C, so $T(\text{K}) = \theta(°\text{C}) + 273$ and $\theta(°\text{C}) = T(\text{K}) - 273$. The degree is the same size on both scales, so a change of temperature is the same number in K as in °C (a rise of 20 °C is a rise of 20 K) — and there are no negative kelvin temperatures. Ice melts at 273 K, water boils at 373 K, room temperature is about 293 K. The kelvin is the SI unit of temperature, and the scale scientists use for gases, because its zero is a real zero: at 0 K the particles have the least possible energy and a gas would exert no pressure.

parts.title: Both ways
parts.question: (a) Convert 25 °C to kelvin. (b) Convert 200 K to degrees Celsius. (c) A gas is heated from 300 K to 350 K; state the temperature change in °C. (3 marks)
steps: (c) A change of 50 K is a change of 50 °C — the degree is the same size on both scales.

questions.text: Convert 37 °C to kelvin.
Convert 77 K (liquid nitrogen) to degrees Celsius.
Describe what is meant by absolute zero. (2)
questions.model:
• The lowest possible temperature, −273 °C (0 K)…
  • …at which the particles have the least possible movement (lowest possible energy) — a gas would exert no pressure.

questions.text: A temperature rise of 15 °C is a rise of…
questions.explain: Changes are the same on both scales; only the zero differs.

questions.text: Which temperature is impossible?
questions.explain: Nothing is below absolute zero.

checklist: Describe absolute zero in terms of particle movement
Convert between kelvin and degrees Celsius
State that a temperature change is the same in K and °C, and that 0 K is the lowest possible temperature
sections.blurb: Cool a gas and its particles slow down; at −273 °C they would have the least possible energy and the pressure would be zero — absolute zero, the bottom of the kelvin scale. Kelvin and Celsius degrees are the same size, so converting is adding or subtracting 273, and a temperature change is the same number on both scales.

sections.title: Compressing a gas: the force on the walls, and P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ at constant temperature

parts.title: Volume down, pressure up
parts.html:
Compressing and expanding (14.16P, 14.17P): a gas has no fixed volume — push a piston in and the same particles fit into a smaller space; let it out and they spread into the larger one. Because the particles collide with every wall, the gas pressure produces a net force at right angles to any surface (the piston, the walls, your eardrum); the force on a surface is pressure × area (Topic 15), which is why a small pressure on a large area is a large force.

The volume chain (14.18P), at constant temperature so the particles' speed is unchanged: a smaller volume means the particles have less distance to travel between the walls, so each particle hits the walls more often (more collisions per second); the collisions are no harder than before (same speed); but there are more of them on a smaller area, so the force per unit area — the pressure — increases. The relationship is exact: $P_1 V_1 = P_2 V_2$ (14.19P), pressure inversely proportional to volume for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature. Pressure can be in any unit as long as both pressures are in the same one (Pa, kPa, atmospheres), and the same for the volumes.

parts.title: The syringe
parts.question: A sealed syringe holds 80 cm³ of air at a pressure of 100 kPa. The plunger is pushed in slowly until the volume is 25 cm³. Calculate the new pressure, and state the assumption you made. (3 marks)
steps: $P_2 = 320$ kPa — the volume is 3.2 times smaller, so the pressure is 3.2 times larger.
Assumption: the temperature stays constant (pushed in slowly, so the gas does not warm up) and no air escapes (fixed mass).

questions.text: A gas occupies 2.0 m³ at 150 kPa. Calculate its volume when the pressure is increased to 300 kPa at constant temperature.
A diver's air bubble has a volume of 5.0 cm³ at a depth where the pressure is 400 kPa. Calculate its volume at the surface, where the pressure is 100 kPa (same temperature).
A fixed mass of gas is compressed to half its volume at constant temperature. Explain, in terms of particles, why its pressure doubles. (3)
questions.model:
• The particles' speed is unchanged (same temperature), but they have less distance to travel between the walls…
  • …so each particle collides with the walls more often — twice as many collisions per second in half the volume (the collisions are not harder).
  • More collisions per second on a smaller wall area means a greater force per unit area: the pressure doubles ($P_1 V_1 = P_2 V_2$).

questions.text: The pressure of a gas produces a force on a surface that is…
options: at right angles to the surface
only on the bottom of the container
questions.explain: 14.17P: a net force at right angles to any surface.

questions.text: $P_1 V_1 = P_2 V_2$ applies only when…
options: the mass of gas is fixed and the temperature is constant
questions.explain: Change the temperature and the speeds change too — the equation no longer holds.

checklist: Explain that a gas can be compressed or expanded by changing the pressure, and that its pressure produces a net force at right angles to any surface
Explain why reducing the volume at constant temperature increases the pressure
Use $P_1 V_1 = P_2 V_2$ for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature
sections.blurb: A gas can be squeezed into a smaller volume or allowed to expand; its pressure exerts a net force at right angles to every surface it touches. Halve the volume of a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature and each particle hits the walls twice as often, so the pressure doubles: pressure × volume stays constant.

sections.title: Key words: state what is meant by…

parts.title: The definitions
parts.html:
"State what is meant by" asks for the definition. Learn these as sentences.

TermWhat to write (mark-scheme form)Not this
DensityMass per unit volume: $\rho = m / V$, in kg/m³."how heavy it is"
Internal energyThe total energy stored in a system by its particles: their kinetic energy (movement) plus their potential energy (positions / bonds)."heat"
Specific heat capacityThe energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C (J/kg °C).missing the 1 kg or the 1 °C
Specific latent heatThe energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of a substance without a change in temperature (J/kg); fusion for melting, vaporisation for boiling.missing "no change in temperature"
Melting point / boiling pointThe temperature at which a substance changes state (solid ↔ liquid; liquid ↔ gas) — the temperature stays constant while it does."when it gets hot"
SublimationA change directly from solid to gas (dry ice, iodine).confusing with evaporation
Physical changeA change in which no new substance is formed (e.g. a change of state); mass is conserved and the original properties return when it is reversed."a change you can see"
Pressure (of a gas)The force per unit area exerted on a surface by the collisions of the gas particles with it."how squashed the gas is"
Absolute zeroThe lowest possible temperature, −273 °C (0 K), at which the particles have the least possible movement (energy)."when everything freezes"
Kelvin scaleThe temperature scale that starts at absolute zero: $T(\text{K}) = \theta(°\text{C}) + 273$; the same size of degree as Celsius.a scale with a different degree size
Thermal insulatorA material with a low thermal conductivity (usually trapping air) that reduces the rate of energy transfer by heating."stops heat"
Conservation of mass (in a change of state)The mass is the same before and after a change of state, because the same particles are present — only their arrangement and movement change."nothing changes"

questions.text: State what is meant by density. (1)
questions.model: • Mass per unit volume (mass ÷ volume).

questions.text: State what is meant by the specific latent heat of fusion of a substance. (1)
questions.model: • The energy needed to change 1 kg of the substance from solid to liquid (melt it) without a change in temperature.

questions.text: Which is the best definition of absolute zero?
options: The temperature at which water freezes
The lowest possible temperature, −273 °C, at which particles have the least possible movement
questions.explain: $-273\ °\text{C} = 0\ \text{K}$; least possible movement.

questions.text: State what is meant by the internal energy of a system. (1)
questions.model: • The total energy stored by its particles: their kinetic energy plus their potential energy.

questions.text: The pressure of a gas on a surface is…
options: the force per unit area from the particles' collisions with the surface
questions.explain: Force per unit area, from the particles' collisions with the surface.

checklist: Define density, internal energy, specific heat capacity and specific latent heat
Define melting and boiling point, sublimation and physical change
Define gas pressure, absolute zero, the kelvin scale and a thermal insulator
sections.blurb: One-mark definitions in the form of words the mark schemes credit. The two that lose marks most are specific heat capacity without the 1 kg and 1 °C, and specific latent heat without "no change in temperature".

sections.title: Particle answers that score: motion, not bulk properties
equations: \text{say what the particles do, not what the stuff does}

parts.title: What scored and what did not
parts.html:
QuestionScoredDid not score
2023 Q3(c)(ii): motion of particles in a liquid (2)"flow over each other"; "move around"; moving with a range of speeds in random directions; "move freely" (1 mark only, says nothing more about the motion)"with lots of energy" (imprecise); "take the shape of the container" (bulk property); descriptions of melting (the wrong question)
2025 Q5(b): change in motion as liquid wax freezes (2)"now only vibrate in fixed positions" (both marks); "no longer move past each other"; "slow down / lose kinetic energy""become closer together" (arrangement, not motion — "not enough for a mark"); a description of melting
2024 Q9(b): heating a gas in a sealed can — which does not changethe mean distance between particles (fixed volume, fixed number)speed, energy, pressure — these all rise

The template for a change of state: before (the motion in the first state) → the joining word ("gain energy and speed up" / "lose energy and slow down") → after (the motion in the second state). Melting: "vibrate about fixed positions → gain energy → leave their fixed positions and move around / flow over each other". Boiling: "move around, touching → gain enough energy to break away from each other → move fast in straight lines, far apart". Condensing and freezing: the same lines read backwards, with "lose energy / slow down". Keep the particles the subject of every sentence: "the particles …", never "the wax …".

parts.title: Boiling, as the particles
parts.question: Water is heated until it boils. Describe the changes in the arrangement and movement of the particles. (3 marks)
steps: Before: in the liquid the particles are touching, in no pattern, and move around / flow past each other at a range of speeds.
Joining: as the water is heated the particles gain energy and move faster, until at the boiling point they have enough energy to break away from their neighbours.
After: in the gas they are far apart and move fast in straight lines in random directions.

questions.text: Steam condenses on a cold window. Describe the change in the motion of the water particles. (2)
questions.model:
• In the steam the particles move fast in straight lines, far apart; on the cold glass they lose energy and slow down.
  • In the liquid they are touching and move around / flow over each other (no longer in straight lines).

questions.text: A question asks about the motion of particles as a liquid freezes. Which answer earns nothing?
options: They now only vibrate in fixed positions
They no longer move past each other
questions.explain: 2025: arrangement, not motion — 'not enough for a mark'.

questions.text: 'The particles have lots of energy' as a description of a liquid's particles is…
options: imprecise — it says nothing about how they move
questions.explain: 2023 report: imprecise phrases scored nothing.

questions.text: Describe the motion of the particles in a solid, and how it changes when the solid is heated but does not melt. (2)
questions.model:
• The particles vibrate about fixed positions.
  • When heated they vibrate faster / with a larger amplitude (more kinetic energy) but stay in their fixed positions.

questions.text: Which sentence keeps the particles as the subject, as the mark scheme wants?
options: The wax gets harder as it cools
The particles slow down and then only vibrate in fixed positions
questions.explain: Say what the particles do, not what the wax does.

checklist: Give the scoring movement phrase for each state
Describe a change of state as a change in motion: before → joining word → after
Avoid the three answers that earn nothing: bulk properties, 'lots of energy', describing a different change
sections.blurb: Two examiners' reports in three years said the same thing: students describe the material (it flows, it takes the shape of the container, it melts) when the question asked about the particles. Each state has one movement phrase that scores; a change of state needs the before, the after and the word that joins them.

sections.title: Density the hard way: rearranging, units, rounding and scale readings

parts.title: The four traps
parts.html:
TrapWhat the examiners sawWhat to do
Rearranging2024 Q3(a): $V = m \div \rho$ — a mark for the substitution or the rearrangement, a mark for the evaluation (1.57 cm³)write the rearranged equation first, then substitute; both earn credit even if the arithmetic slips
Units2023 Q3(b): kg and m³ converted to g and cm³ "with incorrect powers of ten"stay in SI; if you must convert, 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³, 1 cm³ = $10^{-6}$ m³, 1 g = $10^{-3}$ kg
Rounding2025 Q5(c)(i): 0.0047 m³ rounded to 0.005 m³ — "poor practice"keep the significant figures of the data (two or three); never round to one figure
Scale reading2024 Q3(d): a measuring cylinder read before and after (1350 and 1750 cm³) — the volume is the difference, 400 cm³read the bottom of the meniscus on both, subtract, check the unit on the scale

The upthrust route (Topic 15 meets Topic 14, June 2025 Q9(a)): weigh an object in air and in water: the reading falls because of the upthrust — the block's apparent loss in weight in the liquid — which is equal to the weight of liquid displaced (the 2-mark explanation in June 2025 Q9(a)(i)); so the mass of water displaced $= \text{upthrust} \div g$, and its volume = that mass ÷ 1000 kg/m³ — and that is the volume of the object. Then $\rho = m \div V$ for the object (the mass from its weight in air). The scheme gave $1.43 \times 10^{-4}$ m³ and $4.9 \times 10^3$ kg/m³, with error carried forward from the volume into the density.

sections.title: Planning the density practical: the 6-mark method, and the eureka-can trap
equations: \text{mass on a balance; volume by ruler or displacement}
\rho = m \div V \text{ (or the gradient of } m \text{ against } V)

parts.title: The method marks, and the investigation
parts.html:
The method question: the marks are for named apparatus (balance, measuring cylinder, ruler), the readings taken (mass; volume before and after; the dimensions), the processing (subtract the volumes; multiply the dimensions; $\rho = m \div V$) and one accuracy point (meniscus at eye level, fully submerged, dry before weighing, repeat the lengths). The June 2023 report: the measuring-cylinder method with before, after and subtract scored; the displacement (eureka) can "scored nothing" — the question had given a measuring cylinder, and the can is a different method, fine for an object too big for a cylinder but not the one asked for — and measurements "not relevant to volume, such as the metal's mass" earned nothing in a volume question.

StepDoes the density of a material depend on the size of the sample?
1 Variablesindependent: the volume of the sample (different-sized blocks of the same material); dependent: its mass; control: the same material, the same balance, dry samples
2 Relationship$\rho = m \div V$, so $m = \rho V$: mass should be proportional to volume and a graph of $m$ against $V$ a straight line through the origin with gradient = density
3 Changeuse five or more blocks of the material of different sizes (or add identical cubes one at a time)
4 Measuremass with a balance; volume with a ruler ($l \times w \times h$) or by displacement in a measuring cylinder
5 Useplot mass against volume; draw the line of best fit; the gradient is the density; a straight line through the origin shows the density does not depend on size
6 Accuracyzero the balance; measure each length in several places and average; read the meniscus at eye level
7 Repeatrepeat each mass and volume reading and take a mean

parts.title: The 6-mark method
parts.question: Describe how to find the density of an irregular stone and of a sample of oil. (6 marks)
steps: Stone, mass: measure its mass with a balance (zeroed first).
Stone, volume: put water in a measuring cylinder and read the volume; lower the stone in so it is completely submerged; read the new volume; subtract to get the stone's volume.
Oil, mass: put an empty measuring cylinder on the balance and zero it (or record its mass); pour in the oil; read the mass (subtracting the cylinder if needed).
Oil, volume: read the volume of the oil from the cylinder's scale.
Calculate: density = mass ÷ volume for each ($\rho = m / V$).

Accuracy: read the meniscus at eye level; use a cylinder only a little wider than the stone so the rise in level is large; dry the stone before weighing (or weigh it first). ("Repeat and average" is ignored in the density method schemes, 2019 and 2023.)

questions.text: Plan an investigation to find out whether the density of a material depends on the size of the sample. (6)
questions.model:
6 marks — one mark per row below, any 6 of the 7.

PointForWhat you need to write
1VariablesIndependent: the volume (size) of the sample; dependent: its mass; control: the same material, the same balance.
2Relationship$m = \rho V$: mass should be proportional to volume; the gradient of a mass–volume graph is the density.
3ChangeUse at least five samples of the same material of different sizes.
4MeasureMass with a balance; volume with a ruler ($l \times w \times h$) or by displacement in a measuring cylinder (before, after, subtract).
5UsePlot mass against volume; a straight line through the origin shows the density is the same for every size; gradient = density.
6AccuracyZero the balance; measure each length in several places; read the meniscus at eye level; fully submerge.
7RepeatRepeat each reading and take a mean — write it, but know that the density schemes (2019, 2023) ignore it; the accuracy marks are eye level, full immersion and a right-sized cylinder.
  • Any six of the seven points.

questions.text: Why is the object lowered gently so it is completely under the water?

So the full volume of the object is displacing water and none splashes out
So the object does not dissolve
questions.explain: Any part above the water, or any splash, makes the volume reading too small.

  • Use a large volume of liquid (smaller percentage error) / zero the balance with the empty cylinder on it. (Not "repeat and average" — ignored in these schemes.)

The seven-step recipe fits the investigation version: does the density of a material depend on the size of the sample? Mass against volume, and the gradient is the density.

sections.title: Heating and cooling graphs: what a flat section means, and the 2025 cooling-curve marks
equations: \text{flat section: change of state, } Q = m L

parts.title: Reading the graph, and explaining it
parts.html:
Sloping section: the energy supplied raises the temperature — the particles move faster. Flat section: the energy supplied changes the state — it separates the particles (potential energy) and the kinetic energy, and so the temperature, does not change. Its height is the melting or boiling point; its length is how long the change took, so with a steady heater of power $P$, the energy for the change is $E = P t$ and $L = E \div m$. A cooling curve is the same picture upside down: the flat section is freezing (or condensing), at the same temperature as melting, with the energy going out to the surroundings.

The June 2025 report (Q5(c)(iii), a cooling curve for wax with a table of its specific heat capacity and specific latent heat, 3 marks): the marks were for saying that the latent heat is much larger than the specific heat capacity — "much more energy is needed to change state than to change temperature" — quoting the values from the table to support it; and that less energy is transferred to the surroundings while the solid cools (R to S) than while it freezes (Q to R) — the comparison is the mark. A fourth idea, that the rate of transfer is about the same throughout so a larger energy takes a longer time, "was rarely seen". Many candidates "described melting rather than freezing" — on a cooling curve the flat part is the wax freezing.

Why flat sections are long: for water, $L_{\text{fusion}} = 334\,000$ J/kg against $c = 4200$ J/kg °C — melting 1 kg of ice takes as much energy as warming the water by about 80 °C; boiling it ($L_{\text{vap}} = 2\,260\,000$ J/kg) takes over five times more than warming it from 0 to 100 °C.

parts.title: The ice graph
parts.question: The graph shows the temperature of 0.10 kg of ice heated by a 70 W heater. Use the graph to find the specific latent heat of fusion of ice. (3 marks)
steps: The flat section at 0 °C (melting) runs from 1 min to 9 min: $t = 8$ min $= 480$ s.
Energy supplied during melting: $E = P t = 70 \times 480 = 33\,600$ J.

parts.text: Explain why the flat section lasts longer than the time taken to cool from 80 °C to 60 °C. (3)

parts.text: What is happening to the wax between 2 min and 8 min?

It is cooling as a liquid

questions.text: On a heating graph for a steady heater, the energy needed for the change of state is found from…
options: the height of the flat section
power × the length (time) of the flat section
the gradient of the flat section
the time at the end of the flat section
questions.explain: $E = P t$ with t the length, not the end time; in seconds.

questions.text: Why does a cooling curve for a pure substance have a flat section at the same temperature as its heating curve?
options: Freezing happens at the melting point: the same change of state, with the latent heat given out instead of taken in
questions.explain: Melting point = freezing point.

checklist: Read a melting or boiling point and the length of a flat section from a heating or cooling graph
Explain why the temperature stays constant during a change of state
Explain why a flat section is longer than the sloping ones using the latent heat and specific heat capacity values
sections.blurb: A temperature–time graph for a steady heater has sloping parts (the temperature rises, $\Delta Q = m c \Delta \theta$) and flat parts (a change of state at constant temperature, $Q = m L$). Reading the graph is one skill; explaining why the flat part is flat, and why it is long, is where the 2025 marks were lost.

sections.title: Specific heat capacity versus specific latent heat: the comparisons, and "why was the rise smaller?"

parts.title: Comparing, predicting, explaining the shortfall
parts.html:
ShapeHow to answer
Compare: oil $c = 2000$, water $c = 4200$ J/kg °C — same mass, same energy$\Delta\theta = \Delta Q \div (m c)$: the oil's temperature rises more (about 2.1 times as much) because less energy is needed per degree; or, the same temperature rise needs less energy for the oil
Compare: $L_{\text{fusion}}$ (334 kJ/kg) and $L_{\text{vap}}$ (2260 kJ/kg) for waterboiling needs far more energy per kg than melting: the particles must separate completely, not just leave their fixed positions
Predict: 0.50 kg of water receives 21 000 J$\Delta\theta = 21\,000 \div (0.50 \times 4200) = 10$ °C
Explain the shortfall: the measured rise is less than the calculated onesome of the energy is transferred to the surroundings (the air, the bench) and to the container, heater and thermometer, so less energy goes into the water than the heater supplied

The June 2024 scheme (Q9(c)(ii), 2 marks: why the actual rise was smaller than calculated): any two of "not all the energy supplied goes to the brick", "not all of it stays there", "energy transferred to the heater parts", "energy transferred to the surroundings", or the equation argument; "ignore 'energy is lost / wasted' unqualified", "ignore 'not 100 % efficient'" and sound — and the one sentence "the brick transfers thermal energy to the surroundings" scored both marks. Say where the energy went, with a destination. The reverse version — the calculated $c$ comes out too high — has the same cause: the energy you put into $\Delta Q$ was the heater's, but the water only got part of it, so dividing the full energy by the (smaller) rise overestimates $c$.

parts.title: Calculated and measured
parts.question: A 50 W heater runs for 5.0 minutes in 0.25 kg of water ($c = 4200$ J/kg °C). (a) Calculate the expected temperature rise. (b) The measured rise is 11 °C. Explain why. (4 marks)
steps: $\Delta\theta = \Delta Q \div (m c) = 15\,000 \div (0.25 \times 4200) = 14$ °C (14.3).
(b) Some of the heater's energy is transferred to the surroundings (the air and the bench)…
…and some to the beaker, the heater itself and the thermometer, so less than 15 000 J went into the water and its rise is smaller.

questions.text: A 60 W heater runs for 4.0 minutes in 0.20 kg of a liquid. The temperature rises by 30 °C. Calculate the specific heat capacity of the liquid (assume all the energy goes into the liquid).
questions.hint: $E = P t$ first (t in seconds), then $c = E \div (m \Delta \theta)$.

questions.text: In the heater experiment above (60 W for 4.0 minutes, 0.20 kg of liquid, a 30 °C rise), the true specific heat capacity of the liquid is smaller than the value calculated from these figures. Explain why. (2)
questions.model:
• Some of the heater's energy is transferred to the surroundings (air, bench) and to the container, heater and thermometer, so less energy went into the liquid than $P t$.
  • The temperature rise is therefore smaller than it would be for the full energy, and dividing the full energy by the smaller rise gives a value of $c$ that is too large.

questions.text: Equal masses of oil ($c = 2000$ J/kg °C) and water ($c = 4200$ J/kg °C) receive the same energy. Which is true?
options: The oil's temperature rises more, about twice as much
Both rise by the same amount
questions.explain: $\Delta \theta = \Delta Q \div (m c)$: smaller c, bigger rise.

questions.text: Which explanation of a smaller-than-expected temperature rise would the 2024 scheme ignore?
options: Energy was transferred to the surroundings
Energy was transferred to the beaker and heater
questions.explain: 'Not 100 % efficient' and 'energy is lost' were ignored — name the destination.

questions.text: Explain why the specific latent heat of vaporisation of water (2 260 000 J/kg) is much larger than its specific latent heat of fusion (334 000 J/kg). (2)
questions.model:
• Boiling must separate the particles completely (overcome the forces between them so they are far apart), whereas melting only lets them leave their fixed positions while still touching.
  • Separating them fully needs far more energy per kilogram, so $L_{\text{vap}}$ is much larger.

checklist: Compare two substances from their specific heat capacities or latent heats
Calculate a temperature rise from an energy, then explain why the real rise is smaller
Say where the 'missing' energy went in the mark-scheme words
sections.blurb: Three question shapes mix the two quantities: compare two substances from their values, say what happens to a given energy, and explain why the measured temperature rise is smaller than the calculated one. The last has a mark-scheme answer — energy transferred to the surroundings, or to the heater and container — and two phrasings the scheme ignores.

sections.title: The water core practical: the specific heat capacity 6-marker and the melting-ice graph
equations: \Delta Q = E = P t \text{ (or } I V t\text{)}

parts.title: The 2024 levels
parts.html:
The June 2024 scheme (Q9(d), 6 marks): apparatus — immersion heater, power supply, balance, thermometer, stopwatch, joulemeter (or ammeter and voltmeter), insulated container, stirrer; steps — measure the mass of water on the balance; record the initial temperature; switch on and time with the stopwatch; stir; record the final temperature; read the energy from the joulemeter (or $E = I V t$, or $P t$); rearrange $\Delta Q = m c \Delta\theta$ to $c = \Delta Q \div (m \Delta\theta)$; or plot temperature against energy and use the gradient. Level 3 (5–6 marks) needs the temperature change, the energy supplied and how to find $c$ from them; Level 2 is a method with gaps; Level 1 is apparatus with no coherent method. "Ignore Bunsen burner" — the energy from a flame cannot be measured.

StepSpecific heat capacity of water
1 Variablesmeasure: mass of water, initial and final temperature, energy supplied (or current, pd and time); control: lagging, lid, stirring, the same beaker
2 Relationship$\Delta Q = m c \Delta\theta$, so $c = \Delta Q \div (m \Delta\theta)$
3 Changelet the heater run (e.g. 10 minutes), or take readings every minute to plot a graph
4 Measuremass on a balance (zero with the empty beaker); temperatures with the thermometer; energy on the joulemeter or $E = I V t$ with an ammeter, voltmeter and stopwatch
5 Use$c = \Delta Q \div (m \Delta\theta)$; or plot temperature against energy — gradient $= 1 \div (m c)$
6 Accuracylag the beaker and use a lid (less energy to the surroundings); stir so the thermometer reads the whole water; read the thermometer at eye level; keep the heater fully under the water; heat for longer (or use less water) so the temperature rise is larger and its uncertainty matters less
7 Repeattake readings every minute and use the gradient of the graph — in "improve the method" questions "repeat the readings" is ignored (2018, 2020); lid, lagging, stirrer, heater fully under the water and a larger temperature rise are what score

The melting-ice half: crushed ice in a beaker, thermometer in, heat gently (or let it stand), record the temperature every minute. The temperature rises to 0 °C and then stays at 0 °C while the ice melts, though energy is still going in; once it has all melted, the water warms. The flat section is the evidence that a change of state happens at a constant temperature.

parts.title: The Level 3 method
parts.question: Describe a method to find the specific heat capacity of water using an electric heater. (6 marks)
steps: Measure the mass of water in an insulated beaker with a balance (zero the balance with the empty beaker).
Put an immersion heater and a thermometer in the water, with a lid; record the initial temperature.

Switch on the heater and start a stopwatch; after a measured time (say 10 minutes) switch off, stir, keep watching the thermometer and record the highest temperature reached as the final temperature (the water takes time to heat through — the whole of the 3-mark June 2022 Q9(b), and a point in the 2024 and Nov 2021 6-markers).
Measure the energy supplied with a joulemeter, or from the ammeter and voltmeter readings: $E = I V t$.
Calculate the temperature change $\Delta\theta$ = final − initial; then $c = \Delta Q \div (m \Delta\theta)$.
To reduce energy transferred to the surroundings, lag the beaker and use a lid; repeat, or plot temperature against energy and use the gradient.

questions.text: A student puts a beaker of water on a tripod, heats it with a Bunsen burner for five minutes and records the temperature before and after. She says she cannot now calculate the specific heat capacity of the water. Explain why, and describe the changes to her method that would let her find it. (6)
questions.model:
6 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1Why notShe has no value for the energy supplied: a Bunsen burner's energy transfer cannot be measured (and much of it heats the air and the beaker), so $\Delta Q$ in $\Delta Q = m c \Delta\theta$ is unknown — the mass of water may also be unmeasured.
2HeaterReplace the burner with an immersion heater in the water, connected to a power supply through a joulemeter (or an ammeter and voltmeter with a stopwatch so that $E = I V t$).
3MassMeasure the mass of the water with a balance (zeroed with the empty beaker).
4TemperaturesRecord the initial temperature; after heating, switch off, stir, keep watching and record the highest temperature reached: $\Delta\theta$ = final − initial.
5CalculateRearrange: $c = \Delta Q \div (m \Delta\theta)$ — or take readings every minute and plot temperature against energy, using the gradient.
6AccuracyLag the beaker and use a lid so that nearly all the measured energy goes into the water; keep the heater fully under the water. ("Repeat" is ignored in these schemes.)
  • Marked by levels, not per row: Level 3 (5–6) needs the reason (no measured energy), the temperature change, the energy supplied and how $c$ is found from them; Level 2 is a method with gaps.

questions.text: The graph shows the temperature of crushed ice in a beaker as it is heated steadily.

parts.text: Explain the shape of the graph between 1 min and 7 min. (2)
parts.model:
• The ice is melting: the temperature stays at 0 °C (the melting point) while the state changes.
  • The energy supplied goes into separating the particles from their fixed positions (potential energy), not into increasing their speed, so the temperature does not rise.
parts.label: a

parts.text: What does the graph show after 7 min?
options: All the ice has melted and the water is warming up
parts.explain: Once the change of state is complete the energy raises the temperature again.
parts.label: b

graph.alt: Temperature of crushed ice against time while heated: rises from minus 10 to 0 degrees in the first minute, flat at 0 degrees from 1 to 7 minutes, then rises to 30 degrees at 10 minutes.

questions.text: Why is a Bunsen burner not accepted as the heater in this method?

It is not allowed in the lab

questions.text: State two ways to reduce the energy transferred to the surroundings in this experiment, and why that matters. (3)

  • Use a lid (reduces convection and evaporation from the surface).
  • If energy goes to the surroundings the water gets less than the heater supplied, the temperature rise is too small, and the calculated $c$ is too large.

questions.text: In the experiment, 0.50 kg of water rises from 18 °C to 38 °C while the joulemeter reads 44 000 J. Calculate the value of c this gives.
