Say what Level 3 needs: Δθ measured, energy measured or calculated, c from $\Delta Q = m c \Delta \theta$
Describe the melting-ice half and sketch its graph
sections.blurb: Core practical 14.11 has two halves: heat ice and watch the temperature hold at 0 °C while it melts; heat water with an electric heater and find its specific heat capacity. The 2024 paper set the second as a 6-marker and the levels are in the report: Level 3 needs the temperature change, the energy, and how c comes out of them.

sections.title: Explaining gas pressure: temperature, volume, and the force on the walls

parts.title: The two chains side by side
parts.html:
ChangeHeld constantChain
Temperature upvolume (and mass)particles move faster → collide with the walls more often and harder (greater force each) → greater total force on the walls → pressure up
Volume down [P]temperature (and mass)particles have less distance to travel between the walls → collide with the walls more often (same speed, so not harder) → more collisions per second on a smaller area → pressure up; $P_1 V_1 = P_2 V_2$
Force on a surface [P]—collisions exert a force at right angles to the surface; force = pressure × area; a balloon stays inflated because the inside gas pushes out on the rubber more than the outside air pushes in

The common mix-up is a volume answer that says the particles hit "harder" — at constant temperature they do not: same speed, same force per collision, just more of them. The other is forgetting the condition: $P_1 V_1 = P_2 V_2$ needs a fixed mass at constant temperature, and "heating raises the pressure" needs a fixed volume (a sealed rigid container). A balloon in the sun expands instead, because its volume is free to change — and a balloon in a cold room shrinks, for the same reason in reverse.

parts.title: The cold balloon
parts.question: An inflated balloon is left in a cold room overnight and is smaller in the morning. Explain why, in terms of particles. (3 marks)
steps: The air particles inside the balloon lose energy and slow down as the air cools.
They collide with the inside of the balloon less often and less hard, so the force on the rubber from the inside falls.

The balloon is not rigid: the outside air pushes the rubber in until the inside pressure matches again, so it is the volume that decreases (in a sealed rigid can the volume could not change, and the pressure would fall instead).

questions.text: A sealed, rigid can of air is warmed. Explain why the pressure inside it increases. (3)
questions.model:
• The particles gain energy and move faster.
  • They collide with the walls more often and harder (a greater force in each collision).
  • The volume is fixed, so a greater total force on the same area: the pressure increases.

questions.text: The temperature chain and the volume chain both end with a higher pressure. State the one link that is different between them, and why. (2)
questions.model:
• Temperature up (constant volume): the particles hit the walls more often and harder, because they are moving faster.
  • Volume down (constant temperature): the particles hit the walls more often but not harder, because their speed is unchanged — they simply have less distance to travel between the walls.

questions.text: A gas is compressed at constant temperature. Which statement is WRONG?
options: The particles hit the walls more often
The particles hit the walls harder
The particles have less distance to travel between collisions with the walls
questions.explain: Same temperature, same speed, same force per collision.

questions.text: A balloon in the sun gets bigger; a sealed rigid can in the sun gets a higher pressure. Why the difference?
options: The balloon's volume is free to change, so the extra force from the faster particles pushes the rubber out; the can's volume cannot change, so the pressure rises instead
questions.explain: Same chain inside both; what is held constant differs.

questions.text: Explain how the gas in a car tyre exerts a force on the inside of the tyre. (2)
questions.model:
• The gas particles move randomly and collide with the inner surface of the tyre; each collision exerts a small force at right angles to the surface.
  • The total of all the collisions per unit area is the pressure; force = pressure × area on each part of the tyre wall, which holds the tyre's shape.

checklist: Write the temperature chain (constant volume) and the volume chain (constant temperature) without mixing them
Say which single link changes between the two chains
Explain the force a gas exerts on a surface, and why a tyre or balloon holds its shape
sections.blurb: Every gas-pressure explanation is the same chain — particles, collisions with the walls, force, pressure — with one link changed. Temperature changes how fast the particles hit; volume changes how often. Keep the two straight, and say which quantity was held constant. (Doing work on a gas, the Higher Physics step, has the next section to itself.)

sections.title: Doing work on a gas: why a bicycle pump gets warm
equations: \text{work done on the gas} \rightarrow \text{particles rebound faster} \rightarrow \text{KE up} \rightarrow \text{temperature up}

parts.title: The work-done link
parts.html:
StepWhat to write
1pushing the piston in does work on the gas (a force moves through a distance): energy is transferred to the gas
2particles that collide with the moving piston rebound faster than they arrived (like a ball hit by a moving bat)
3the particles' average kinetic energy increases
4so the temperature of the gas increases — nothing heated it; the energy came in as work
5(if asked about the pressure) the faster particles hit the walls more often and harder, and the volume is smaller so they hit more often for that reason too — the pressure rises by more than $P_1 V_1 = P_2 V_2$ predicts, because the temperature is not constant

The reverse happens too: a gas that expands and pushes a piston out does work on the piston, its particles rebound from the retreating piston more slowly, and its temperature falls — which is why an aerosol can feels cold as it empties and why a bicycle tyre's air cools as it is let out. The spec statement is 14.20P: "explain why doing work on a gas can increase its temperature, including a bicycle pump" — Higher Physics only.

parts.title: The bicycle pump
parts.question: A bicycle pump is used with its outlet blocked. The handle is pushed in quickly. Explain why the air inside becomes hotter and its pressure rises. (4 marks)
steps: Pushing the handle in does work on the air: the moving piston transfers energy to the particles that collide with it, so they rebound faster.
The particles' kinetic energy increases, so the temperature of the air rises (the pump feels warm).
The faster particles collide with the walls more often and harder, so the pressure rises…
…and the volume is smaller, so the particles also hit the walls more often because they have less distance to travel — both effects raise the pressure.

questions.text: In a diesel engine the air in the cylinder is compressed very quickly by the piston and becomes hot enough to ignite the fuel. Explain why the air gets so hot. (3)
questions.model:
• The piston moving in does work on the air: energy is transferred to the gas.
  • Particles colliding with the moving piston rebound faster than they arrived, so the particles' kinetic energy increases.
  • A higher average kinetic energy of the particles is a higher temperature — and the compression is so quick that little energy is transferred to the surroundings meanwhile.

questions.text: 'Doing work on a gas' means…
options: heating the gas with a flame
a force (the piston) moving through a distance into the gas, transferring energy to it
questions.explain: Work = force × distance, into the gas.

questions.text: The air let out of a bicycle tyre feels cold. Explain why, in terms of the particles. (2)
questions.model:
• The escaping air expands and does work pushing the surrounding air out of the way: energy is transferred from the gas.
  • Its particles lose kinetic energy (they rebound more slowly from the retreating boundary), so the temperature falls.

questions.text: A gas is compressed quickly to half its volume. Compared with compressing it slowly at constant temperature, the final pressure is…
options: the same — $P_1 V_1 = P_2 V_2$ always
higher, because the work done has also raised the temperature, so the particles hit harder as well as more often
questions.explain: Quick compression: the temperature is not constant, so the equation underestimates the pressure.

checklist: Explain why doing work on a gas increases its temperature
Explain why a gas compressed quickly ends up at a higher pressure for two reasons
Say what 'doing work on the gas' means in terms of the piston and the particles
sections.blurb: Push a piston in and you do work on the gas: the particles bounce off the moving piston faster than they arrived, their kinetic energy rises, and so does the temperature — a bicycle pump warms up even though nothing is heating it. The chain has one step the temperature chain in the last section does not: where the energy came from.

sections.title: Kelvin traps: changes, negatives, and when °C is fine

parts.title: The four traps
parts.html:
TrapRight
"The temperature rose from 20 °C to 50 °C. What is the rise in K?" — answered 303 KA change is the same on both scales: 30 K. Only an actual temperature gets the 273.
A calculated temperature of −20 KImpossible: 0 K is the lowest temperature. Check the arithmetic (probably subtracted 273 from a value that was already in kelvin, or added where you should have subtracted).
Converting to kelvin before using $\Delta Q = m c \Delta\theta$Not needed: the equation uses the change, which is the same in °C. Converting both temperatures and subtracting gives the same $\Delta\theta$; converting only one is wrong by 273.
"40 °C is twice as hot as 20 °C"No: the Celsius zero is just the freezing point of water, not zero energy. 20 °C → 40 °C is 293 K → 313 K, about 7 % more. Only the kelvin scale starts where the particles have the least possible movement, so only kelvin values can be compared as ratios.

Why the kelvin scale matters: its zero is absolute zero, where the particles have the least possible movement and a gas would exert no pressure. On the Celsius scale that point is −273 °C, so Celsius values can be negative and cannot be compared as multiples; kelvin values can. Converting is only ever adding or subtracting 273.

parts.title: All three at once
parts.question: Liquid nitrogen boils at 77 K. (a) Convert this to °C. (b) A sample is warmed from 77 K to 20 °C; find the temperature rise in K. (c) A student writes the rise as 216 °C and the final temperature as −56 K. Say what is wrong with each. (4 marks)
steps: (c) The rise of 216 K is also a rise of 216 °C — that part is right, because a change is the same on both scales.
But −56 K is impossible: no temperature is below 0 K. The student has subtracted 273 from a value that was already in kelvin; the final temperature is 293 K (20 °C).

questions.text: Water is heated from 15 °C to 65 °C. State the temperature rise in kelvin.
questions.hint: A change is the same on both scales.

questions.text: A gas is cooled from 450 K to −23 °C. Calculate the fall in temperature in kelvin.
questions.hint: Convert −23 °C to K first, then subtract.

questions.text: A student finds a temperature of −30 K in a calculation. This means…
options: a mistake — no temperature is below 0 K
questions.explain: Absolute zero is the floor.

questions.text: 0.50 kg of water is warmed from 10 °C to 30 °C ($c = 4200$ J/kg °C). The correct energy calculation is…
questions.explain: $\Delta\theta = 20$ °C $= 20$ K; converting only one temperature is wrong by 273.

questions.text: Explain why 40 °C is not 'twice as hot' as 20 °C, and state the scale on which such a comparison would make sense. (2)
questions.model:
• The Celsius zero (the freezing point of water) is not zero energy: the particles still have plenty of movement at 0 °C, so Celsius values cannot be compared as ratios (20 °C → 40 °C is 293 K → 313 K).
  • The kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, where the particles have the least possible movement, so only kelvin values can be compared as multiples.

checklist: Leave a temperature change alone when switching scales
Spot an impossible temperature
Explain why only the kelvin scale has a real zero
sections.blurb: Four small things cost kelvin marks: converting a temperature change (don't — it is the same number), writing a negative kelvin temperature (impossible), adding 273 to a Celsius value inside $\Delta Q = m c \Delta \theta$ (unnecessary, and wrong if you do it to only one of the two temperatures), and treating a Celsius value as if doubling it doubled anything physical.

facts.q: Movement of particles in a solid?
facts.a: Vibrate about fixed positions.

facts.q: Movement of particles in a liquid (the phrase that scores)?
facts.a: Move around / flow past each other, in random directions, at a range of speeds, colliding with each other (still touching) — 2023: any two of random / range of speeds / collide / faster than a solid.

facts.q: Movement of particles in a gas?
facts.a: Fast, in straight lines, in random directions; far apart; colliding with each other and the walls.

facts.q: Arrangement in a solid, liquid, gas?
facts.a: Solid: regular, touching, fixed positions. Liquid: irregular, touching, no fixed positions. Gas: random, far apart.

facts.q: Why can a gas be compressed but a liquid cannot?
facts.a: Gas particles are far apart with empty space between them; liquid particles are already touching.

facts.q: Density equation and SI unit?
facts.a: $\rho = m \div V$; kg/m³.

facts.q: 1 g/cm³ in kg/m³?
facts.a: 1000 kg/m³ (multiply g/cm³ by 1000).

facts.q: Density of water?
facts.a: About 1000 kg/m³ (1 g/cm³).

facts.q: Units advice from the 2023 report?
facts.a: Use SI units unless told to convert; converting to g and cm³ went wrong with powers of ten.

facts.q: Rounding advice from the 2025 report?
facts.a: Keep the significant figures of the data; rounding 0.0047 m³ to 0.005 m³ was 'poor practice'.

facts.q: Volume of a regular block?
facts.a: Measure length, width and height with a ruler; $V = l \times w \times h$.

facts.q: Volume of an irregular solid?
facts.a: Measuring cylinder: read the water volume, lower the object in fully submerged, read again, subtract.

facts.q: Mass and volume of a liquid?
facts.a: Empty measuring cylinder on a balance, zero it, pour in the liquid: mass from the balance, volume from the scale.

facts.q: The eureka-can trap?
facts.a: When the question gives a measuring cylinder, describe that method: in 2023 a displacement can scored nothing there.

facts.q: Accuracy points for the cylinder method?
facts.a: Read the bottom of the meniscus at eye level; fully submerge; lower gently; dry before weighing or weigh first.

facts.q: Why is a solid usually denser than its liquid?
facts.a: Particle spacing is smaller — more particles per unit volume; same mass per particle.

facts.q: Why is a gas about 1000 times less dense than a liquid?
facts.a: Particles far apart (about ten times further in each direction): far fewer per m³.

facts.q: The exception to 'solid denser than liquid'?
facts.a: Ice is less dense than water (open lattice) — it floats.

facts.q: The six changes of state?
facts.a: Melting, freezing, boiling/evaporating, condensing, sublimating (solid → gas), deposition (gas → solid).

facts.q: Why is mass conserved in a change of state?
facts.a: The same particles are present before and after — none created or destroyed; only arrangement and movement change.

facts.q: Physical change vs chemical change?
facts.a: Physical: no new substance, reversible, original properties recovered. Chemical: new substances formed.

facts.q: Boiling vs evaporating?
facts.a: Boiling: throughout the liquid at the boiling point. Evaporating: from the surface at any temperature.

facts.q: Which changes give energy out?
facts.a: Freezing and condensing (and deposition).

facts.q: Two things heating can do to a system?
facts.a: Raise its temperature (particles move faster, KE up) or change its state (particles separate, PE up, temperature constant).

facts.q: Define specific heat capacity.
facts.a: The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C.

facts.q: Define specific latent heat.
facts.a: The energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of a substance without a change in temperature.

facts.q: Difference between SHC and SLH?
facts.a: SHC: temperature change, no change of state. SLH: change of state, no temperature change.

facts.q: SHC of water?
facts.a: 4200 J/kg °C — large, so water heats and cools slowly.

facts.q: Latent heats of water?
facts.a: Fusion 334 000 J/kg; vaporisation 2 260 000 J/kg.

facts.q: Equation for a temperature change?
facts.a: $\Delta Q = m c \Delta\theta$ — Δθ is the change, same in °C or K.

facts.q: Equation for a change of state?
facts.a: $Q = m L$ — no Δθ; fusion or vaporisation as appropriate.

facts.q: Ice at −10 °C to water at 20 °C: how many stages?
facts.a: Three: warm the ice (c of ice), melt it ($L_f$), warm the water (c of water); add.

facts.q: Heater running for a time: first step?
facts.a: $E = P t$ (t in seconds), then the thermal equation.

facts.q: How does thermal insulation work?
facts.a: Low thermal conductivity, usually by trapping air (poor conductor, cannot convect in pockets): slower conduction and convection.

facts.q: Examples of thermal insulation?
facts.a: Lagging, loft and cavity-wall insulation, double glazing, a lid, a vacuum flask.

facts.q: Cable's plastic coating — thermal insulation?
facts.a: No: electrical insulation. Waste heating in a cable is reduced by lowering its resistance (2025).

facts.q: How does a vacuum flask reduce transfer?
facts.a: No particles in the vacuum: no conduction or convection; silvered surfaces reduce radiation.

facts.q: Why does a gas exert a pressure?
facts.a: Particles move fast and randomly, collide with the walls; each collision exerts a force; total force per unit area is the pressure.

facts.q: Heating a gas at constant volume: the chain?
facts.a: Particles faster → collide with the walls more often and harder → greater total force → pressure increases.

facts.q: Which statement earns nothing about gas pressure?
facts.a: 'Particles collide with each other more' — only collisions with the walls count.

facts.q: Sealed can heated: what does not change?
facts.a: The mean distance between particles (fixed volume, fixed number).

facts.q: What is absolute zero?
facts.a: The lowest possible temperature, −273 °C (0 K): particles have the least possible movement; gas pressure would be zero.

facts.q: °C to K?
facts.a: Add 273. K to °C: subtract 273.

facts.q: A temperature change of 20 °C in kelvin?
facts.a: 20 K — changes are the same on both scales.

facts.q: Melting and boiling points of water in K?
facts.a: 273 K and 373 K.

facts.q: Reducing volume at constant temperature: the chain?
facts.a: Less distance between walls → more frequent collisions (same speed, not harder) → higher pressure.

facts.q: The equation for a gas at constant temperature?
facts.a: $P_1 V_1 = P_2 V_2$ — fixed mass, constant temperature.

facts.q: Direction of the force a gas exerts on a surface?
facts.a: At right angles to the surface; force = pressure × area.

facts.q: Template for a change-of-state motion answer?
facts.a: Before (motion in state 1) → joining word (gain/lose energy, speed up/slow down) → after (motion in state 2); particles as the subject.

facts.q: Three answers that earn nothing about particle motion?
facts.a: Bulk properties (takes the shape of the container), 'lots of energy', and describing a different change (melting when asked about freezing).

facts.q: Volume from an upthrust?
facts.a: The apparent loss in weight in the liquid = upthrust = weight of water displaced; mass of water $= \text{upthrust} \div g$; volume = mass ÷ 1000 kg/m³ = object's volume.

facts.q: Measuring-cylinder volume of an object?
facts.a: Final reading − initial reading.

facts.q: Mass–volume graph for one material?
facts.a: A straight line through the origin; gradient = density; shows density does not depend on size.

facts.q: Flat section on a heating graph?
facts.a: A change of state at constant temperature: height = melting/boiling point; length × power = energy for the change.

facts.q: Why is the flat section long (2025)?
facts.a: Latent heat ≫ specific heat capacity (quote the values); less energy leaves during the cooling section than during freezing; energy leaves at about the same rate throughout, so the larger energy takes longer.

facts.q: Flat section on a cooling curve?
facts.a: Freezing (or condensing) — not melting; same temperature as the melting point; energy given out.

facts.q: Why was the measured temperature rise smaller than calculated (2024)?
facts.a: Not all the energy supplied goes to / stays in the object: energy transferred to the surroundings and to the heater parts. 'Energy is lost' scores only with a destination; 'not 100 % efficient' is ignored.

facts.q: Same energy, same mass, smaller c?
facts.a: Larger temperature rise: $\Delta\theta = \Delta Q \div (m c)$.

facts.q: SHC-of-water practical: apparatus?
facts.a: Immersion heater, power supply, balance, thermometer, stopwatch, joulemeter (or ammeter and voltmeter), insulated beaker with lid, stirrer.

facts.q: SHC-of-water practical: Level 3 needs?
facts.a: The temperature change, the energy supplied (joulemeter or $I V t$), and $c = \Delta Q \div (m \Delta\theta)$.

facts.q: Why not a Bunsen burner?
facts.a: The energy it supplies cannot be measured.

facts.q: Melting-ice half of the practical shows?
facts.a: Temperature holds at 0 °C while the ice melts even though energy is supplied: a change of state at constant temperature.

facts.q: Why does a bicycle pump get warm?
facts.a: Work is done on the gas; particles rebound from the moving piston faster; their KE and the temperature rise.

facts.q: Air let out of a tyre feels cold — why?
facts.a: The expanding gas does work on its surroundings; its particles lose KE; the temperature falls.

facts.q: Volume chain: harder or more often?
facts.a: More often only — same temperature, same speed, same force per collision.

facts.q: A balloon in the sun vs a sealed can in the sun?
facts.a: Same chain inside; the balloon's volume is free to change so it expands, the can's is fixed so its pressure rises.

facts.q: Is 40 °C twice as hot as 20 °C?
facts.a: No: the Celsius zero is not zero energy (293 K → 313 K). Only kelvin values can be compared as ratios.

facts.q: Converting to kelvin inside $\Delta Q = m c \Delta\theta$?
facts.a: Not needed — the equation uses the change, the same in °C and K; converting only one temperature is wrong by 273.

facts.q: State what is meant by: density.
facts.a: Mass per unit volume: $\rho = m / V$, in kg/m³.

facts.q: State what is meant by: internal energy.
facts.a: The total energy stored in a system by its particles: their kinetic energy (movement) plus their potential energy (positions / bonds).

facts.q: State what is meant by: specific heat capacity.
facts.a: The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C (J/kg °C).

facts.q: State what is meant by: specific latent heat.
facts.a: The energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of a substance without a change in temperature (J/kg); fusion for melting, vaporisation for boiling.

facts.q: State what is meant by: melting point / boiling point.
facts.a: The temperature at which a substance changes state (solid ↔ liquid; liquid ↔ gas) — the temperature stays constant while it does.

facts.q: State what is meant by: sublimation.
facts.a: A change directly from solid to gas (dry ice, iodine).

facts.q: State what is meant by: physical change.
facts.a: A change in which no new substance is formed (e.g. a change of state); mass is conserved and the original properties return when it is reversed.

facts.q: State what is meant by: pressure (of a gas).
facts.a: The force per unit area exerted on a surface by the collisions of the gas particles with it.

facts.q: State what is meant by: absolute zero.
facts.a: The lowest possible temperature, −273 °C (0 K), at which the particles have the least possible movement (energy).

facts.q: State what is meant by: kelvin scale.
facts.a: The temperature scale that starts at absolute zero: $T(\text{K}) = \theta(°\text{C}) + 273$; the same size of degree as Celsius.

facts.q: State what is meant by: thermal insulator.
facts.a: A material with a low thermal conductivity (usually trapping air) that reduces the rate of energy transfer by heating.

facts.q: State what is meant by: conservation of mass (in a change of state).
facts.a: The mass is the same before and after a change of state, because the same particles are present — only their arrangement and movement change.

types.name: Density
types.method: Density is mass divided by volume. Decide which unit the question wants: grams with cm³ gives g/cm³, kilograms with m³ gives kg/m³. If you are given the sides of a cuboid, multiply length × width × height to get the volume first, then divide the mass by it.
commonErrors: Dividing volume by mass instead of mass by volume
Mixing grams with m³, or kilograms with cm³, in the same calculation
Forgetting that 1 m³ is 1 000 000 cm³ (not 100 cm³) when converting

worked.question: A block of aluminium has a mass of 540 g and a volume of 200 cm³. Calculate the density of aluminium in g/cm³.
steps: Known: m = 540 g, V = 200 cm³. Unknown: ρ.
ρ = m / V
ρ = 2.7 g/cm³

practice.question: A pebble has a mass of 150 g. When it is lowered into a measuring cylinder the water level rises by 60 cm³. Calculate the density of the pebble in g/cm³.
practice.hint: The rise in water level is the volume of the pebble; use ρ = m / V.
walkthrough: m = 150 g, V = 60 cm³, find ρ.

practice.question: A lorry delivers 3 m³ of concrete with a total mass of 7200 kg. Calculate the density of the concrete in kg/m³.
practice.hint: Divide the mass in kg by the volume in m³.
walkthrough: m = 7200 kg, V = 3 m³, find ρ.

practice.question: Olive oil has a density of 0.92 g/cm³. Calculate the mass of the oil in a full 500 cm³ bottle. Give your answer in g.
practice.hint: Rearrange ρ = m / V to m = ρ × V.
walkthrough: ρ = 0.92 g/cm³, V = 500 cm³, find m.
ρ = m / V → m = ρ × V

practice.question: The density of air is 1.2 kg/m³. The air in a small office has a mass of 60 kg. Calculate the volume of the office in m³.
practice.hint: Rearrange ρ = m / V to V = m / ρ.
walkthrough: ρ = 1.2 kg/m³, m = 60 kg, find V.
ρ = m / V → V = m / ρ

practice.question: A house brick measures 20 cm by 10 cm by 6 cm and has a mass of 2.16 kg. Calculate the density of the brick in g/cm³.
practice.hint: Find the volume from length × width × height, change the mass to grams, then divide.

practice.question: A steel bolt has a volume of 25 cm³ and a mass of 0.195 kg. Calculate the density of steel in kg/m³.
practice.hint: Change 25 cm³ to m³ by dividing by 1 000 000, then use ρ = m / V.

types.name: Specific heat capacity
types.method: Thermal energy transferred equals mass × specific heat capacity × change in temperature. Work out the temperature change Δθ first (final minus start), make sure the mass is in kg, then multiply. To find c, m or Δθ, divide ΔQ by the other two.
commonErrors: Using the final temperature instead of the temperature change
Leaving the mass in grams, which makes the answer 1000 times too big
Forgetting to change kJ to J before dividing

worked.question: A pan holds 2 kg of water at 20 °C. Calculate the energy needed to heat the water to 70 °C. Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg °C.
steps: Known: m = 2 kg, c = 4200 J/kg °C, Δθ = 70 − 20 = 50 °C. Unknown: ΔQ.
ΔQ = m × c × Δθ

practice.question: An empty aluminium saucepan of mass 1.5 kg is heated on a hob from 15 °C to 115 °C. Calculate the energy transferred to the pan. Specific heat capacity of aluminium = 900 J/kg °C.
practice.hint: Find Δθ = 115 − 15 first, then use ΔQ = m × c × Δθ.

practice.question: A 0.5 kg copper block in a school experiment warms up by 40 °C. Calculate the energy transferred to the block. Specific heat capacity of copper = 390 J/kg °C.
practice.hint: The temperature change is given directly; multiply m × c × Δθ.

practice.question: A 2 kg iron weight in a gym is left in the sun and gains 50 000 J of energy. Its temperature rises by 50 °C. Calculate the specific heat capacity of iron.
practice.hint: Rearrange to c = ΔQ / (m × Δθ).
walkthrough: ΔQ = 50 000 J, m = 2 kg, Δθ = 50 °C, find c.
ΔQ = m × c × Δθ → c = ΔQ / (m × Δθ)

practice.question: A mug contains 250 g of water. A microwave transfers 42 000 J of energy to the water. Calculate the rise in temperature of the water. Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg °C.
practice.hint: Change 250 g to kg, then rearrange to Δθ = ΔQ / (m × c).
walkthrough: m = 250 g = 0.25 kg, ΔQ = 42 000 J, c = 4200 J/kg °C, find Δθ.

practice.question: A 2 kW kettle contains 1 kg of water. It is switched on for 105 s. Calculate the rise in temperature of the water, assuming all the energy goes into the water. Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg °C.
practice.hint: First find the energy from E = P × t (2 kW = 2000 W), then use Δθ = ΔQ / (m × c).
walkthrough: Energy supplied: E = P × t = 2000 × 105 = 210 000 J

practice.question: A 3 kW immersion heater warms 60 kg of water in a hot-water tank from 15 °C to 55 °C. Calculate the time this takes in seconds, assuming no energy is wasted. Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg °C.
practice.hint: Find the energy needed with ΔQ = m × c × Δθ, then use t = E / P with P = 3000 W.

types.name: Specific latent heat
types.method: The energy to change the state of a substance, with no change in temperature, is mass × specific latent heat. Use the latent heat of fusion for melting or freezing and the latent heat of vaporisation for boiling or condensing. Keep the mass in kg; to find m or L, divide Q by the other one.
commonErrors: Using the latent heat of fusion for boiling, or vaporisation for melting
Including a temperature change: there is none while the state is changing
Leaving the mass in grams

worked.question: Calculate the energy needed to melt 0.5 kg of ice at 0 °C. Specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 334 000 J/kg.
steps: Known: m = 0.5 kg, L = 334 000 J/kg. Unknown: Q.
Q = m × L

practice.question: A pan of 2 kg of water at 100 °C is left boiling until it has all turned to steam. Calculate the energy transferred to the water. Specific latent heat of vaporisation of water = 2 260 000 J/kg.
practice.hint: The water is boiling, so use the latent heat of vaporisation in Q = m × L.
walkthrough: m = 2 kg, L = 2 260 000 J/kg, find Q.

practice.question: A freezer turns 1.5 kg of water at 0 °C into ice at 0 °C. Calculate the energy the freezer removes from the water. Specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 334 000 J/kg.
practice.hint: Freezing releases the same energy as melting would take: Q = m × L with the latent heat of fusion.
walkthrough: m = 1.5 kg, L = 334 000 J/kg, find Q.

practice.question: A steam iron transfers 1 130 000 J of energy to boil water into steam. Calculate the mass of water boiled. Specific latent heat of vaporisation of water = 2 260 000 J/kg.
practice.hint: Rearrange Q = m × L to m = Q / L.
walkthrough: Q = m × L → m = Q / L

practice.question: It takes 52 500 J of energy to melt 300 g of candle wax at its melting point. Calculate the specific latent heat of fusion of the wax.
practice.hint: Change 300 g to kg, then rearrange to L = Q / m.
walkthrough: Q = m × L → L = Q / m

practice.question: A 1.5 kW kettle is left boiling for 4 minutes. Calculate the mass of water that boils away in this time, assuming all the energy goes into making steam. Specific latent heat of vaporisation of water = 2 260 000 J/kg.
practice.hint: First find the energy from E = P × t with the time in seconds, then use m = Q / L.

practice.question: A 400 W heater is used to melt 2 kg of ice at 0 °C. Calculate the time it takes to melt all the ice, in seconds, assuming all the energy goes into the ice. Specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 334 000 J/kg.
practice.hint: Find the energy needed with Q = m × L, then use t = E / P.

types.name: Heating with a change of state
types.method: When a substance is heated through a melting or boiling point there are two parts: a temperature change (use ΔQ = m × c × Δθ) and a change of state at constant temperature (use Q = m × L). Work out each part separately and add them. If a heater is involved, the total energy equals power × time.
commonErrors: Only doing one of the two parts
Using the temperature change in the latent heat part: the state changes at one temperature
Forgetting to change minutes to seconds when a power is given

worked.question: A drink contains 0.5 kg of ice at 0 °C. Calculate the total energy needed to melt the ice and then warm the water to 20 °C. Specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 334 000 J/kg. Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg °C.
steps: Total = 209 000 J

practice.question: A pan holds 2 kg of water at 80 °C. Calculate the total energy needed to heat the water to 100 °C and then boil all of it into steam. Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg °C. Specific latent heat of vaporisation of water = 2 260 000 J/kg.
practice.hint: Warming part: m × c × Δθ with Δθ = 20 °C. Boiling part: m × L. Add them.

practice.question: A 0.2 kg block of ice at 0 °C is taken from a freezer, melted and the water warmed to 40 °C. Calculate the total energy transferred to the ice. Specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 334 000 J/kg. Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg °C.
practice.hint: Melt first (m × L), then warm the water (m × c × Δθ) and add.

practice.question: A kettle contains 500 g of water at 60 °C. Calculate the total energy needed to heat the water to 100 °C and boil all of it away. Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg °C. Specific latent heat of vaporisation of water = 2 260 000 J/kg.
practice.hint: Change 500 g to 0.5 kg, then add the warming energy and the boiling energy.

practice.question: A tray holds 0.4 kg of water at 30 °C. It is put in a freezer, cooled to 0 °C and frozen solid. Calculate the total energy removed from the water, in kJ. Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg °C. Specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 334 000 J/kg.
practice.hint: Cooling part: m × c × Δθ with Δθ = 30 °C. Freezing part: m × L. Add, then divide by 1000 for kJ.

practice.question: A 2 kW heater is used to melt 1 kg of ice at 0 °C and then warm the water to 30 °C. Calculate the time this takes in seconds, assuming all the energy goes into the ice and water. Specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 334 000 J/kg. Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg °C.
practice.hint: Find the total energy (melt + warm), then t = E / P with P = 2000 W.

practice.question: A camping stove heats 1.5 kg of water from 60 °C to 100 °C and then boils all of it away. This takes 25 minutes. Calculate the useful power of the stove in W. Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg °C. Specific latent heat of vaporisation of water = 2 260 000 J/kg.
practice.hint: Find the total energy (warm + boil), change 25 minutes to seconds, then P = E / t.

types.name: Temperature scales
types.method: To change °C to kelvin add 273; to change kelvin to °C subtract 273. Absolute zero is 0 K, which is −273 °C. A change in temperature is the same number in °C and in K, so do not add 273 to a temperature difference.
commonErrors: Subtracting 273 when changing °C to K
Adding 273 to a temperature change
Writing °K: the kelvin has no degree sign

worked.question: A laboratory is at 25 °C. Convert this temperature to kelvin.
steps: Known: 25 °C. Unknown: the temperature in K.
Temperature = 298 K

practice.question: Water boils at 100 °C at normal atmospheric pressure. Convert this temperature to kelvin.
practice.hint: Add 273 to the Celsius temperature.

practice.question: Absolute zero is 0 K, the lowest possible temperature. Give absolute zero in °C.
practice.hint: Subtract 273 from the kelvin temperature.

practice.question: The temperature in a cold store for frozen food is −40 °C. Convert this temperature to kelvin.
practice.hint: Add 273 to −40, keeping the minus sign in mind.

practice.question: A gas in a sealed container is warmed from 20 °C to 80 °C. Calculate the change in its temperature in kelvin.
practice.hint: A temperature change is the same size in °C and in K; do not add 273.
walkthrough: A change of 60 °C is a change of 60 K

practice.question: A gas in a bicycle pump is at 27 °C. It is heated until its kelvin temperature has doubled. Calculate its new temperature in °C.
practice.hint: Change 27 °C to kelvin, double it, then change back to °C.

practice.question: A kitchen is at 22 °C. The inside of the freezer is at 255 K. Calculate the difference in temperature between the kitchen and the freezer, in °C.
practice.hint: Change 255 K to °C first, then subtract it from 22 °C.

types.name: Gas pressure and volume at constant temperature
types.method: For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, pressure × volume stays the same. Write down P₁ and V₁ before the change and P₂ or V₂ after, multiply P₁ × V₁, then divide by the one you know to find the one you do not. Any units work as long as both pressures match and both volumes match.
commonErrors: Mixing kPa with Pa, or cm³ with litres, on the two sides of the equation
Multiplying P₁ by V₂ instead of pairing the before values together
Expecting the volume to go up when the pressure goes up: they move in opposite directions

worked.question: A gas has a volume of 600 cm³ at a pressure of 100 kPa. It is compressed slowly to 200 cm³ at the same temperature. Calculate the new pressure in kPa.
steps: Known: P₁ = 100 kPa, V₁ = 600 cm³, V₂ = 200 cm³. Unknown: P₂.
P₁ × V₁ = P₂ × V₂ → P₂ = P₁ × V₁ / V₂
P₂ = 300 kPa

practice.question: A sealed syringe contains 50 cm³ of air at 100 kPa. The plunger is pushed in until the volume is 20 cm³, with no change in temperature. Calculate the new pressure of the air in kPa.
practice.hint: P₂ = P₁ × V₁ / V₂; the volume goes down so the pressure goes up.
walkthrough: P₁ = 100 kPa, V₁ = 50 cm³, V₂ = 20 cm³, find P₂.

practice.question: An air bubble of volume 2 cm³ is released by a diver where the pressure is 300 kPa. It rises to the surface, where the pressure is 100 kPa. Calculate the volume of the bubble at the surface in cm³, assuming the temperature stays the same.
practice.hint: V₂ = P₁ × V₁ / P₂; the pressure drops so the bubble grows.
walkthrough: P₁ = 300 kPa, V₁ = 2 cm³, P₂ = 100 kPa, find V₂.

practice.question: A party balloon holds 1.5 litres of air at 100 kPa. It is squeezed until the pressure inside is 120 kPa at the same temperature. Calculate the new volume of the balloon in cm³. (1 litre = 1000 cm³)
practice.hint: Change 1.5 litres to cm³ first, then use V₂ = P₁ × V₁ / P₂.

practice.question: A diver's cylinder has a volume of 12 litres. When all the air inside is released at a pressure of 100 kPa it fills 2400 litres. Calculate the pressure of the air in the cylinder in kPa, assuming constant temperature.
practice.hint: Rearrange to P₁ = P₂ × V₂ / V₁; both volumes are already in litres.
walkthrough: V₁ = 12 litres, P₂ = 100 kPa, V₂ = 2400 litres, find P₁.

practice.question: A bicycle pump contains 240 cm³ of air at 100 kPa. The handle is pushed in until the pressure is 160 kPa, with no change in temperature. Calculate the decrease in the volume of the air in cm³.
practice.hint: Find the new volume from V₂ = P₁ × V₁ / P₂, then subtract it from 240 cm³.

practice.question: A gas cylinder has a cross-sectional area of 20 cm². A piston traps a column of gas 15 cm long at a pressure of 100 kPa. The piston is pushed in until the column is 5 cm long, at the same temperature. Calculate the new pressure in kPa.
practice.hint: Volume = area × length; find V₁ and V₂ first, then use P₂ = P₁ × V₁ / V₂.

types.name: Reading a heating graph
types.method: A heating graph shows temperature against time while a heater supplies energy at a steady rate. A flat section is a change of state: its height is the melting or boiling point and its length is the time the change takes. Multiply that time (in seconds) by the heater power to get the energy for the change of state. On a sloping section the gradient is the rate of temperature rise; power = m × c × gradient, so c = P / (m × gradient).
commonErrors: Reading the time at the end of the flat section instead of its length
Leaving the time in minutes when multiplying by a power in watts
Taking the gradient of the flat section, which is zero, instead of a sloping section

worked.question: A sample of wax is heated at a steady rate. The graph shows how its temperature changes with time. Use the graph to determine the melting point of the wax.
steps: The melting point is the temperature of the flat section, where the wax changes state without warming up.
The flat section runs from 4 min to 8 min.
Reading across to the temperature axis, the flat section is at 60 °C.
Melting point = 60 °C

graph.alt: Temperature–time graph rising from 20 °C to 60 °C over 4 minutes, flat at 60 °C until 8 minutes, then rising to 100 °C at 12 minutes

practice.question: A liquid is heated in a beaker by a heater supplying energy at a steady rate. The graph shows its temperature against time. Use the graph to determine the boiling point of the liquid.
practice.hint: The boiling point is the temperature of the flat section, where the temperature stops rising.
walkthrough: The temperature rises until 3 min and then stays constant: the liquid is boiling.
Reading across from the flat section to the temperature axis gives 80 °C.

graph.alt: Temperature–time graph rising from 20 °C to 80 °C over 3 minutes and then flat at 80 °C to 10 minutes

practice.question: A block of ice from a freezer is heated at a steady rate. The graph shows its temperature against time. Use the graph to determine the time, in seconds, that the ice spends melting.
practice.hint: Melting happens along the flat section at 0 °C; find the time at each end of it and subtract.
walkthrough: The flat section at 0 °C starts at 60 s and ends at 540 s.

graph.alt: Temperature–time graph rising from −10 °C to 0 °C in 60 s, flat at 0 °C until 540 s, then rising to 5 °C at 600 s

practice.question: A kettle heats water at a steady rate. The graph shows the temperature of the water against time. Use the graph to determine the rise in temperature of the water during the first 2 minutes.
practice.hint: Read the temperature at 0 min and at 2 min from the sloping line, then subtract.
walkthrough: At 2 min (the dashed line) the temperature is 60 °C.

graph.alt: Temperature–time graph rising from 20 °C to 100 °C over 4 minutes then flat at 100 °C, with a dashed line marking 2 minutes

practice.question: A solid is heated by a 30 W heater. The graph shows its temperature against time. Use the graph to determine the energy supplied by the heater while the solid is melting.
practice.hint: Find how long the flat section lasts, change it to seconds, then use E = P × t.
walkthrough: The flat section runs from 2 min to 7 min, so melting takes 5 min.

graph.alt: Temperature–time graph rising from 20 °C to 50 °C in 2 minutes, flat at 50 °C until 7 minutes, then rising to 80 °C at 10 minutes

practice.question: A 0.4 kg block of a solid is heated by a 40 W heater. The graph shows its temperature against time. Use the gradient of the first straight section of the graph to determine the specific heat capacity of the solid.
practice.hint: Gradient = temperature rise / time; then power = m × c × gradient, so c = P / (m × gradient).
